result.explanation: The insurer rejected the claim under the pre-existing diseases clause on page 30, which excludes expenses related to pre-existing conditions until 36 months of continuous coverage have elapsed. However, the policy was continuously active from January 15, 2020, until the admission date of June 10, 2026, amounting to over 76 months of continuous coverage. Since the 36-month waiting period expired well before the hospital admission, this exclusion cannot justify the claim rejection. Furthermore, because coverage exceeded 60 continuous months, the moratorium period clause on page 37 protects the policyholder from claim contests based on non-disclosure, unless the insurer establishes intentional fraud.
result.what_would_change_it: Evidence that the policy suffered a break in continuity during its term, reducing the active continuous coverage period prior to admission to under 36 months.

arguments.insurer_position: Under the pre-existing diseases clause on page 30 and the pre-existing disease definition on page 7, expenses related to the treatment of a pre-existing disease and its direct complications are excluded from coverage until 36 months of continuous coverage have elapsed. Furthermore, coverage for any pre-existing condition after the 36-month period is subject to the condition having been declared at the time of application and accepted by the insurer.
arguments.claimant_position: The claimant has maintained continuous coverage since January 15, 2020, meaning over 76 months elapsed prior to the June 10, 2026 admission. Under the pre-existing diseases clause on page 30 and the waiting period clause on page 11, the mandatory 36-month waiting period for pre-existing conditions has long expired. Furthermore, under the moratorium period clause on page 37, the policy has passed sixty continuous months of coverage, rendering the claim incontestable on grounds of non-disclosure or pre-existing conditions.
arguments.insurer_weak_point: The policy was incepted on January 15, 2020, and admission occurred on June 10, 2026, meaning over 6 years (76 months) of continuous coverage have passed, far exceeding the 36-month waiting period as well as the 60-month moratorium period.
arguments.claimant_weak_point: The insurer could argue that under the pre-existing diseases clause on page 30, coverage after 36 months is contingent on the condition having been declared at application, or attempt to prove established fraud to bypass the moratorium period.

result.explanation: The pre-existing diseases exclusion clause on page 30 excludes coverage for pre-existing conditions and their direct complications until 36 months of continuous coverage have elapsed from the policy inception date. With your policy commencing on January 1, 2025, and admission occurring in June 2026, only 17 months of continuous coverage had passed at the time of your angioplasty. Provided the insurer has medical evidence that your cardiac condition was diagnosed or treated prior to policy inception, the rejection under the 36-month waiting period is supported by the policy wording. However, the exclusion cannot stand if the condition arose for the first time after your policy began.
result.what_would_change_it: Medical evidence showing the heart condition was first diagnosed after January 1, 2025, or a policy schedule showing ported prior coverage credits or an opted reduced 12-month waiting period.

arguments.insurer_position: Under the pre-existing disease clause on page 7 and the waiting period clause on page 11, pre-existing conditions and their treatments are excluded from coverage until all mandatory waiting periods are completed. The pre-existing diseases exclusion clause on page 30 mandates a waiting period of 36 months of continuous coverage from the policy inception date before expenses related to pre-existing diseases and their direct complications become payable. Because the policy commenced on January 1, 2025, and the angioplasty took place in June 2026, only 17 months of coverage had elapsed, rendering the claim non-payable under the policy terms.
arguments.claimant_position: If the angioplasty treatment arose from underlying chronic conditions such as high blood pressure or cholesterol, it is covered under the ABCD Chronic Care clause on page 69 after a 30-day waiting period, which was fully satisfied between policy inception on January 1, 2025, and admission in June 2026. Furthermore, if the policyholder transferred prior continuous coverage credits under the portability clause on page 7 or elected a reduced waiting period under the PED waiting period modification clause on page 26, the standard 36-month exclusion period is reduced or waived. Consequently, the insurer cannot summarily reject the claim under the standard pre-existing disease exclusion without accounting for these specific coverage terms.
arguments.insurer_weak_point: The insurer bears the burden of proving that the insured's cardiac condition requiring angioplasty was actually diagnosed, treated, or advised upon prior to policy inception to qualify as a pre-existing disease.
arguments.claimant_weak_point: The insurer may argue that angioplasty is a procedure for coronary artery disease rather than direct management of blood pressure or cholesterol, and that the claimant has provided no evidence of an opted PED modification or ported prior continuous coverage to shorten the 36-month waiting period.

result.explanation: The insurer's decision to cap the payout for cataract surgery is supported by the policy terms. Under the cataract treatment provisions on page 9 and page 22, expenses for cataract surgery are strictly capped at 25% of the sum insured or Rs. 40,000 per eye in a single policy year, whichever is lower. Because the total bill of Rs. 95,000 exceeds this maximum allowable sub-limit, the insurer is not required to pay the remaining balance.
result.what_would_change_it: Proof that the surgery was conducted on both eyes during the policy year, which would allow the claimant to claim up to Rs. 40,000 separately for each eye.

arguments.insurer_position: The insurer rightfully partially settled the claim for cataract surgery in accordance with the cataract treatment clause on page 9 and page 22, which caps expenses for cataract treatment at 25% of the Sum Insured or Rs. 40,000, whichever is lower, per eye in a policy year. Under the sub-limit clause on page 8 and the other expenses clause on page 8, the insurer is expressly not liable to pay any amount exceeding this pre-defined limit. Consequently, the claimed amount of Rs. 95,000 was correctly restricted to the maximum allowable sub-limit under the policy.
arguments.claimant_position: The claimant's cataract surgery is a covered procedure under the surgery or surgical procedure clause on page 7, having satisfied the 24-month waiting period required under the specified disease / procedure waiting period clause on page 11. Under the cataract treatment clause on page 9, the insurer is obligated to indemnify medical expenses incurred up to 25% of the Sum Insured or Rs. 40,000 per eye, subject only to the 5% deduction under the co-payment clause on page 10. The claimant is therefore entitled to the full admissible payout up to the policy sub-limit rather than any further reduced settlement.
arguments.insurer_weak_point: The insured may argue that if the surgery involved both eyes or if the sum insured calculation allows for higher coverage, restricting the claim strictly to the Rs. 40,000 cap without clarifying the per-eye application creates an ambiguity that should be resolved in favor of the policyholder.
arguments.claimant_weak_point: The insurer can object that under the sub-limit clause on page 8 and the cataract treatment clause on page 9, policy liability is strictly capped at Rs. 40,000 per eye, making the insurer legally exempt from paying any portion of the Rs. 95,000 claim that exceeds this cap.

result.explanation: The pre-existing disease exclusion clause on page 10 requires 36 months of continuous policy coverage before treatments for pre-existing medical conditions are eligible for reimbursement. Because your policy began on January 1, 2025, and your admission took place in June 2026, only around 17 months of coverage have elapsed under this policy. However, the insurer can only enforce this 36-month waiting period if there is proof that your cardiac condition was diagnosed or treated before the policy start date, or if you lack ported coverage credits from a previous health insurance policy. If the condition arose for the first time after your policy started, this exclusion cannot be used to deny your claim.
result.what_would_change_it: Medical records showing the heart condition was first diagnosed after January 1, 2025, or proof of prior continuous health insurance ported from another policy to fulfill the 36-month waiting period.

arguments.insurer_position: Under the pre-existing diseases exclusion clause on page 10 and the pre-existing disease definition on page 6, expenses related to the treatment of a pre-existing disease and its direct complications are excluded from coverage until 36 months of continuous policy coverage have elapsed. Because the policy commenced on January 1, 2025, and the insured was admitted for angioplasty in June 2026, only about 17 months of coverage have passed. Consequently, the claim falls within the applicable 36-month waiting period and was correctly repudiated.
arguments.claimant_position: Under the pre-existing disease definition on page 6, an ailment is considered pre-existing only if medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment was received within 36 months prior to policy commencement. Furthermore, the pre-existing diseases clause on page 10 and the portability clause on page 17 require the insurer to credit any prior continuous coverage towards reducing the 36-month waiting period. Additionally, Angioplasty is not listed as a restricted procedure under the specified disease waiting period clause on page 11.
arguments.insurer_weak_point: The insurer must present medical evidence proving that the insured was actually diagnosed with or received medical advice/treatment for the underlying cardiac condition prior to policy inception to qualify it as a pre-existing disease.
